claims.text: In its wave sense, displacement is the distance of a point of the medium from its rest position at a given instant, counted positive on one side and negative on the other; amplitude is the maximum displacement, a fixed number for a steady wave.

claims.text: The period T is the time one complete oscillation takes, in seconds; the frequency f is the number of complete oscillations per unit time, in hertz; they are linked by T = 1 ÷ f.

verification.method: Authored originally for topic 7 of the 9702 AS Physics workspace under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Wavelength is the distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase, such as neighbouring crests; phase difference states, in degrees or radians, how far one oscillation leads or lags another as a fraction of a cycle.

claims.text: Displacement and amplitude are not the same quantity: displacement changes from moment to moment and passes through zero, whereas amplitude is the largest displacement and stays constant for a steady wave; the test is whether the quantity changes from moment to moment.

claims.text: The time-base of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) is the time the spot takes to cross one horizontal division of the screen; its setting is read as seconds per division, or milliseconds per division.

claims.text: The y-gain of a CRO is the vertical scale in volts per division; the peak-to-peak voltage is the trace height in divisions multiplied by the y-gain, and the amplitude is the peak-to-peak voltage divided by two.

claims.text: On a CRO trace, the period is the number of horizontal divisions occupied by one complete cycle multiplied by the time-base setting, and the frequency then follows from f = 1 ÷ T.

claims.text: The wave equation v = fλ states that the wave speed v, in m s⁻¹, equals the frequency f, in hertz, multiplied by the wavelength λ, in metres; it follows from the fact that in one period the wave profile advances one wavelength.
